To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.

title: The Power of Sampling for Finding Far-Apart Bases in Matroids
summary:
We study the geometry of matroids via the \emph{diameter} and \emph{dispersion} of the metric space of their bases. Given a matroid $M$, we ask if the diameter of its basis-exchange graph $\mathcal{G}(M)$ can be approximated by sampling two uniformly random bases. As our main result, we show that their expected distance is always at least $1/16$ of the diameter of $\mathcal{G}(M)$. While this might appear to follow from the edge-expansion properties established by Anari, Liu, Gharan and Vinzant (STOC'19), we show that this inutition is false by constructing a graph $G$ with edge-expansion at least $1$ for which sampling two random vertices does \emph{not} give a constant-factor approximation to its diameter.
  We turn to finding $k\geq 2$ maximally-diverse bases of a matroid, the $k$ (max--min) diversity problem. When $k=2$, the problem is solvable via matroid intersection. However, for $k\geq 3$ no polynomial-time approximation or hardness is known, even for diverse spanning trees. We show that sampling $k\geq 3$ bases provides a tight $Θ(\log k)$ approximation. We then combine structural insights about the local density of $\mathcal{G}(M)$ with classical LP-rounding techniques to obtain a polynomial-time $1/6$-approximation algorithm for the $k$-diversity problem in arbitrary matroids, the first constant-factor polynomial-time approximation for max--min diversity on any matroid.
  A key ingredient for our result is the \emph{Farthest Matroid Basis} problem: given a collection of bases, find a new basis as far as possible from all of them. We give a polynomial-time $1/3$-approximation algorithm for this, which is our main algorithmic primitive for $k$ max--min diversity. We also show it is $W[1]$-hard when parameterized by the optimal distance. We also improve the $1/6$-approximation for $k$-diversity, for partition matroids and graphic matroids of constant arboricity.

title: What Must a Model Tell a Planner? Outcome Interfaces for Risk-Aware Planning After Robot Damage
summary: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.

title: One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands
summary:
In the nearest neighbour model of DNA/RNA binding, the partition function (PF) is a sum of Boltzmann-weighted free energies of the exponentially large set of secondary structures. Dirks et al. [SIAM review, 2007] gave a polynomial time PF algorithm for $O(1)$ strands, generalising McCaskill [Biopolymers, 1990] single-stranded case. Despite the intuition that PF may somehow encode the entire state space, thus far different approaches were required to solve various energy-landscape prediction problems. For example: finding the minimum free energy (MFE), structure(s) for $O(1)$ strands was open since 2007, and we recently solved [ICALP, 2025] via new techniques.
  We asked if there is a magnifiable PF algorithm [DNA31, 2025], which we answer here in the affirmative. We give an $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space algorithm, for $c=O(1)$ strands of $N$ bases, the same overhead as Dirks et al. (non-magnifiable) algorithm. However, we show that magnification allows for efficient decoding of the entire landscape, concretely: a single call to the magnifiable PF efficiently solves and improves upon a large number of problems, giving:
  - MFE in $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space; a considerable improvement over our $O(N^4(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^4)$ space result [ICALP 2025].
  - The first polynomial time algorithm for the multi-stranded density of states problem, in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space.
  - The first polynomial time algorithm outputting the entire list of energy levels occupied by at least one structure (in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space), and the first algorithms for various energy landscape and counting problems.
  Our approach unifies the field of energy landscape prediction showing that a single, general, algorithmic framework neatly unifies a large collection of problems that practitioners care about, and required distinct techniques with worse time bounds.

title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
summary: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).

title: Perceived Differences in Activity and Experience Between Developing Software With and Without AI
summary: The fundamental changes in software engineering driven by generative AI will have profound effects not only on the number of available software engineering jobs but also on what software engineering itself looks like. As the career evolves, questions arise about what the skillset and interests of the next generation of software engineers will be and whether long-time engineers will continue to be attracted to the career. In this paper, we contribute to answering these questions by studying how software development with AI tools is perceived to differ from traditional development and how the differences are modulated by years of programming experience. We find that, in terms of programming activities, engineers report less talking with peers about technical problems, less decomposition, less searching of documentation, and less using a debugger, while they report more task switching. We also find experiential differences, including less deep focus and less sense of control over code and design. We call these the different craft results, in contrast to core code-production activities such as writing, refactoring, and fixing code, which show only small mean differences. We also find that these differences are amplified by years of programming experience (an experience gradient), with software engineers who started programming before the age of generative AI perceiving greater changes in both activity and developer experience. We discuss our findings and their implications on training of the next generation of engineers and on engineers who may have difficulty transitioning to the AI-infused world of software engineering.

title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.

title: Real-time neuromorphic audio and vision perception for autonomous robotic applications: Integration and experimental evaluation on a rover platform
summary: Neuromorphic sensing and computing offer a promising alternative to conventional deep learning pipelines for mobile robots, where perception must run continuously under tight latency and energy constraints. However, most neuromorphic solutions are still evaluated offline or on isolated benchmarks, and their integration into complete robotic systems remains largely unexplored. In this technical report, a four-wheel rover platform is presented that combines three real-time perception pipelines: a classical audio tagging pipeline based on Pretrained Audio Neural Networks (PANNs) running on an NVIDIA Jetson GPU, a neuromorphic audio pipeline in which a spiking neural network (SNN) is deployed on the SynSense Xylo Audio~2 chip, and a neuromorphic vision pipeline in which events from an event-based camera are processed by the SpikeYOLO spiking detector for traffic cone detection. On the Xylo chip, the whole processing chain---from the microphone signal to the classification of low- and high-pitched sounds---is performed on-chip, while the host only configures the device and reads the output neurons. All models are deployed as containerised services and integrated through ROS~2, and a configurable action dispatcher maps the detected classes to robot behaviours, closing the loop between perception and actuation. The platform is demonstrated in a proof-of-concept scenario in which the robot reacts to sound classes detected by both audio pipelines and detects traffic cones with the event camera, showing the feasibility of integrating neuromorphic hardware into a multimodal robotic platform operating in real time.

title: Cluster Editing in Subexponential Fixed-Parameter Time
summary:
Cluster Editing asks whether at most $k$ edge additions and deletions turn a given $n$-vertex graph into a disjoint union of cliques. For more than a decade, the fastest algorithm for it was the golden-ratio algorithm of Böcker with running time $O(1.62^k+n^{O(1)})$. Cao and Chen had conjectured that the subexponential running time $2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$ is possible, but this contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself.
  Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.

title: Load-Following Dynamics of an SMR-Powered All-Electric Ship with Battery Energy Storage
summary: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are being considered as compact, high-energy-density power sources for future all-electric ships. In such systems, propulsion-load variations can propagate through the electrical network, turbine-generator set, steam generator, and reactor, producing coupled nuclear, thermal, mechanical, and electrical transients. This paper presents an integrated dynamic load-following analysis of an SMR-powered all-electric ship with and without battery energy storage system (BESS) support. The model couples an integral pressurized water reactor, a once-through moving-boundary steam generator, a simplified turbine model, a synchronous generator, an AC shipboard electrical network, an asynchronous propulsion motor, and a grid-connected BESS. A propulsion-load reduction is applied through the motor torque command, and the responses of the SMR-alone and SMR+BESS configurations are compared. The results show that, without BESS support, the sudden decrease in propulsion motor power creates a temporary surplus between turbine mechanical power and electrical demand, causing a large over-frequency transient and rapid steam-cycle adjustment. With BESS support, the battery absorbs excess electrical power during the transient, reducing the frequency peak from approximately 61.1 Hz to about 60.06 Hz. The BESS also indirectly smooths the upstream steam-cycle and reactor responses, including steam flow, steam-generator pressure, feedwater flow, coolant temperature, reactivity, reactor thermal power, and steam-generator region lengths. These results demonstrate the importance of modeling nuclear-powered electric ships as coupled multi-domain systems and show that BESS integration can improve short-term load-following performance.

title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
comments: 38 pages, 15 figures, 19 tables. Under review at ICLR 2027. Project page: https://kadenzheng.com/model-carving/
summary: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

title: Non-penetrating World Models
summary: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
summary:
To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming.
  To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones. In contrast, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data drop to 25.9% word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and outperforms ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.

title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs is NP-complete
summary: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed $k\geq 3$ has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.

title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design
summary: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.

title: Convergence of a finite element Chorin projection method for the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations
summary: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. We show solvability and uniform moment estimates for the intermediate and the corrected velocity approximations under the assumption that the initial data is square-integrable and divergence free, and that the deterministic forcing term is bounded in $L^{q}(0,T;H^{-1}(D))$ for a sufficiently large $q$. Under standard stability and approximation assumptions on the finite element spaces and a coupling condition on the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, we prove convergence of a subsequence to a martingale solution of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations. The analysis combines the complementary spatial and temporal estimates of the predicted and the corrected velocity approximations and uses the numerical dissipation to identify their common limit. We establish tightness of the piecewise constant temporal interpolations of the velocity field approximations using Aldous' criterion combined with the uniform discrete moment estimates. The convergence result holds in two and three space dimensions as it does not rely on any additional regularity of the limiting martingale solution beyond the one naturally available from the energy inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the scheme in numerical experiments in two space dimensions for smooth and vortex sheet initial data.

title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
comments: 28 pages, 7 figures. EEG dataset (v1.0.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21982978 EEG preprocessing and feature extraction software with XGBoost example (v1.1.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24399993
summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures. EEG dataset (v1.0.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21982978 EEG preprocessing and feature extraction software with XGBoost example (v1.1.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24399993

title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
summary: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.

title: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression,RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting:Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial DeepLearning
summary: This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006-2025 dataset that includes fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit of common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodologies: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today's close as tomorrow's close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement.

title: Nanoscale single-electron box with a floating lead for quantum sensing: modelling and device characterization
summary: We present an in-depth analysis of a single-electron box (SEB) biased through a floating node technique that is common in charge-coupled devices (CCDs). The device is analyzed and characterized in the context of single-electron charge-sensing techniques for integrated silicon quantum dots (QD). The unique aspect of our SEB design is the incorporation of a metallic floating node, strategically employed for sensing and precise injection of electrons into an electrostatically formed QD. To analyse the SEB, we propose an extended multi-orbital Anderson impurity model (MOAIM), adapted to our nanoscale SEB system, that is used to predict theoretically the behaviour of the SEB in the context of a charge-sensing application. The validation of the model and the sensing technique has been carried out on a QD fabricated in a fully depleted silicon on insulator (FDSOI) process on a 22-nm technological node. We demonstrate the MOAIM's efficacy in predicting the observed electronic behavior and elucidating the complex electron dynamics and correlations in the SEB. The results of our study reinforce the versatility and precision of the model in the realm of nanoelectronics and highlight the practical utility of the metallic floating node as a mechanism for charge injection and detection in integrated QDs. Finally, we identify the limitations of our model in capturing higher-order effects observed in our measurements and propose future outlooks to reconcile some of these discrepancies.

title: Ensuring Grid-Safe Forwarding of Distributed Flexibility in Sequential DSO-TSO Markets
summary: This paper investigates sequential flexibility markets consisting of a first market layer for distribution system operators (DSOs) to procure local flexibility to resolve their own needs (e.g., congestion management) followed by a second layer, in which the transmission system operator (TSO) procures remaining flexibility forwarded from the distribution system layer as well as flexibility from its own system for providing system services. As the TSO does not necessarily have full knowledge of the distribution grid constraints, this bid forwarding can cause an infeasibility problem for distribution systems, i.e., cleared distribution-level bids in the TSO layer might not satisfy local network constraints. To address this challenge, we introduce and examine three methods aiming to enable the grid-safe use of distribution-located resources in markets for system services, namely: a corrective three-layer market scheme, a bid prequalification/filtering method, and a bid aggregation method. Technically, we provide conditions under which these methods can produce a grid-safe use of distributed flexibility. We also characterize the efficiency of the market outcome under these methods. Finally, we carry out a representative case study to evaluate the performances of the three methods, focusing on economic efficiency, grid-safety, and computational load.

title: Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network
summary: Topological Deep Learning (TDL) is designed to learn features associated not only with nodes but also with edges, triangles and higher dimensional simplices. However, most TDL approaches, being based on boundary operators and Hodge Laplacians, have the limitation that features and signals cannot be lifted or lowered across more than one dimension per layer. To overcome this limitation, in this work, we propose the adoption of the cup and cap products. Specifically, we formulate the Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network (CCNN), a topological deep learning architecture designed to learn node-based variables (or 0-cochains) by taking into account their many-body interactions (e.g. triangles) present in the data. We validate CCNN by assessing its performance on the TopoBench datasets, demonstrating its competitive performance with respect to other simplicial complex neural networks.

title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
summary: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,μ$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,μ$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,μ$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
summary: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

title: SDG: State-Dependent Gating at Chunk Boundaries for Linear Attention
summary: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.

title: VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows
comments: 26 pages, 3 figures, 16 tables. Accepted at ACM ICAIF 2026 (7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance, Milan). The first 9 pages are the conference paper; Appendices A-K are extra. Code and prompts: https://github.com/datafox-tw/icaif-verifiquant
summary: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 16 tables. Accepted at ACM ICAIF 2026 (7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance, Milan). The first 9 pages are the conference paper; Appendices A-K are extra. Code and prompts: https://github.com/datafox-tw/icaif-verifiquant

title: Distributional Deep Hedging
summary: Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.

title: MambaSplit: Severity-Robust and Inference-Efficient Semantic Unmixing of Fluorescence Microscopy Image Data
comments: 28 pages, 15 figures, 23 tables; main paper (8 pages) followed by supplementary material
summary: The number of structures fluorescence microscopy can image in one sample is limited by how few fluorophores can be separated without significant spectral overlap. Semantic unmixing circumvents this limit by imaging two structures in one fluorescent channel and computationally separating the superimposed image into one image per structure. Because pixels rarely identify their structure, unmixing requires both local and long-range spatial context. The relative brightness of the two structures is unknown and can be very uneven, so predictions must remain accurate across mixing severities, from balanced mixtures to ones where a structure is barely visible. Existing methods either process small image patches or add context through auxiliary pathways that slow inference on large images. We present MambaSplit, a hierarchical state-space encoder with a convolutional decoder that captures context across large tiles in linear time and predicts both channels in one deterministic pass. MambaSplit trains either on computationally summed channel images with random mixing ratios, where a lightweight head estimates the unknown ratio and conditions the decoder on it, or on experimentally acquired superpositions. Across five datasets and nine mixing ratios, MambaSplit achieves the highest RI-PSNR, by up to 3.0 dB, in 11 of 15 dataset-severity combinations and ties in one more, while running 5.9x faster than the strongest baseline. On acquired superpositions, fine-tuning a model pretrained on summed inputs matches or exceeds all baselines. Ablations show that accuracy and robustness come mainly from the training recipe: large tiles, mixing ratios sampled across their full range (up to 11 dB over fixed-ratio training), and independently drawn channel crops (3.9 dB on BioSR). The state-space backbone makes large tiles affordable, enabling high-content screening and event-driven smart microscopy.
comment: 28 pages, 15 figures, 23 tables; main paper (8 pages) followed by supplementary material

title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
summary: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.

title: Pharos: Learning to Control Rare Events at Scale
summary: Rare events drive transformations across physics, chemistry and biology, yet predicting their mechanisms and rates remains a fundamental challenge. Here we introduce Pharos, a framework that learns to make rare transitions accessible while predicting how frequently they occur under physical dynamics. Through stochastic optimal control, Pharos jointly learns the probability of completing a transition and how to steer simulations toward it, allowing sampling and learning to improve one another. Across biomolecular benchmarks, Pharos learns accurate transition probabilities with order-of-magnitude gains in convergence speed over previous algorithms. It transfers across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent while maintaining accurate reaction rate predictions, scales to host-guest binding systems that span millisecond timescales, and enables chemical reaction studies with a computationally demanding machine learning interatomic potential. By combining efficient sampling, quantitative kinetics, and transferability, Pharos opens a route toward foundation models of rare event mechanisms and rates across molecular systems.

title: Avoiding squares over words with lists of size three
summary:
We prove that every sequence of lists of size three admits an infinite square-free word, establishing that the Thue choice number of the path is three. More precisely, the number of compatible square-free words of length $n$ is at least $c(5/4)^n$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant.
  The proof combines a computer-assisted construction of weights with the weighted counting method previously introduced by the author. We first consider words avoiding only squares of bounded period and use a finite state model to certify a uniform lower bound on their growth. The counting argument then controls the loss caused by excluding longer squares. The main new ingredient is a coarser description of the states, which makes the computation feasible without restricting the union of the lists.
  The same computation yields a deterministic polynomial-time strategy for constructing an infinite square-free word when each list is chosen adversarially after the preceding letters have been fixed.

title: A boundary integral equation solver for capsule suspensions
summary: Deformable capsules serve as models for biological cells, such as red blood cells, as well as for synthetic capsules in biomedical and industrial applications. In this work, we introduce a framework for fast and robust simulation of deformable capsules in three-dimensional Stokes flow, both in unbounded domains and in pipe-confined geometries. We solve the Stokes equations using a boundary integral formulation, employing a partition-of-unity discretization for the capsule membrane and the trapezoidal rule with regularization to handle the singular quadrature. Dense periodic interactions are evaluated via a fast Ewald summation scheme, achieving $O(N \log N)$ complexity for $N$ grid points. The interfacial forces on the capsule membrane are modeled using the Skalak constitutive law. We carry out a spectral analysis of this model for small perturbations of a spherical capsule, which indicates that the relaxation dynamics are intrinsically stable. However, the nonlinear character of the Skalak model induces aliasing errors that can compromise numerical stability. To address this when needed, we perform de-aliasing through upsampling and spectral filtering, and we derive guidelines for choosing appropriate filter parameters, thereby stabilizing the method. We investigate the stability and convergence behavior of the resulting scheme and conduct simulations of long-time dynamics, focusing on the relaxation of unconfined capsules and the lateral migration of pipe-confined capsules under various flow conditions.

title: Nonholonomic Event-Triggered Source Seeking
summary: This paper introduces an event-triggered source seeking control (ET-SSC) strategy for autonomous vehicles modeled as nonholonomic unicycles. The key feature of the proposed design is the separation between the continuous probing motion required for gradient extraction and the event-triggered update of the source-seeking correction. This separation enables aperiodic computation and transmission of the correction while the periodic probing signals remain continuously active. The triggering mechanism acts on a low-pass-filtered gradient estimate, obtained by high-pass (washout) filtering, demodulation, and low-pass filtering of the measured signal, and combines a relative and an absolute threshold. Stability is proved with a time-periodic Lyapunov function constructed along the exponentially stable periodic solution of the filtered closed loop, establishing practical exponential convergence of the vehicle to a neighborhood of the unknown source. The guaranteed minimum dwell time is strictly positive and independent of the probing frequency, which excludes Zeno behavior. Unlike available Lie-bracket analyses of the forward-velocity design, the proposed averaging-based analysis accommodates anisotropic quadratic source fields with distinct spatial curvatures. The resulting ET-SSC framework therefore provides a resource-aware implementation in which the source-seeking correction is updated aperiodically while the information-generating probing motion remains continuous.

title: Polynomial sequences of Simplex pivots on 0/1-polytopes
summary:
We study the number of Simplex pivots needed to solve linear programs over $0/1$-polytopes, starting from an arbitrary feasible basis and counting degenerate pivots. It has been known since the 1990s that from any extreme point of a 0/1-polytope there exists a monotone path of linear length to an optimal one. However, translating this into a polynomial sequence of Simplex pivots, i.e., improving basis exchanges, has remained an open question.
  We here provide an affirmative answer, showing that for every 0/1-polytope $\mathcal P \subseteq \mathbb R^d$, an optimal basis can be reached with $O(d^3)$ Simplex pivots, independently of the number of inequalities and of the size of the coefficients.

title: Optimized solver algorithms for computing $\mathrm{Tr}(A^{-1})$
comments: 9 pages, 5 figures. To be published in the proceedings of LATTICE 2026
summary: Estimating the trace of the inverse of a large quark matrix is a longstanding problem in lattice QCD. The standard approach is Hutchinson's method, which uses random noise vectors to estimate the trace to a desired statistical tolerance. Each noise vector $b$ requires solving a system of linear equations $Ax = b$. In this work, we introduce a new class of Krylov solvers for this task, called Twin methods. Twin methods generate the Krylov polynomial once then reuse it on all other right-hand sides. This reduces the number of basic linear algebra operations in the algorithm and therefore lowers the trace computation time. We apply the Twin approach to BiCG and BiCGStab and test them on lattice QCD matrices of varying size and in a range of computing contexts. We also present a more economical estimation of $\mathrm{Tr}(A^{-1})$ which implements a polynomial approximation of $A^{-1}$ and a singular value deflation. In this scheme, the solvers are applied to only a few noise vectors, and the remainder are treated by the polynomial and the deflation. In our tests, the polynomial approximation combined with the deflation yield a 17-fold speedup in the time required to compute the trace over standard Hutchinson's method.
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. To be published in the proceedings of LATTICE 2026

title: A High-Compression Transformer VAE for Efficient and Controllable 3D Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Transformers
summary: Many medical image processing tasks, such as completing missing regions or correcting acquisition artifacts, can be cast as volumetric generation conditioned on observations of the same patient. Diffusion Transformers offer scalable capacity and flexible conditioning for this setting, but they operate on a learned image representation that must preserve fine anatomical and pathological detail while keeping complete three-dimensional volumes tractable. We bring Transformer variational autoencoding and multimodal diffusion together to address this challenge. Trained on BrainTumor-256K, a 249M Transformer VAE encodes and decodes $256^3$ volumes 7.6x faster than a comparably sized CNN trained on the same collection. Their PSNR difference is near zero with training-sized crop inputs, but the Transformer leads by 0.749 dB with full-volume inputs and an unchanged scoring region. Increasing Transformer capacity to 499M improves PSNR across all four brain MRI evaluation sets while retaining 3.8x lower encoding-decoding latency than the CNN. Fast encoding also allows conditions to be constructed dynamically in image space during latent diffusion training. Within the compressed representation, a shared Diffusion Transformer integrates text and spatial references for volumetric synthesis, completion and restoration. The brain-trained autoencoder further transfers to non-brain MRI and CT without target-domain fine-tuning, extending its use beyond the anatomy and modality on which it was learned. The framework provides a reusable representation and conditioning interface for efficient, controllable medical image generation. Code is available at https://github.com/OncoMMAI/brainmri-vit-vae3d.

title: AI-Assisted Decision Support for Formula 1 Pit-Stop Strategy: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Programming
comments: 54 pages (main text and appendices). Code, data and trained models: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24361704
summary: Pit-stop strategy in Formula 1 is a sequential decision problem under uncertainty, in which strategists decide at each lap whether to pit and which tire compound to fit. We develop a data-driven simulator, calibrated with historical race data, that captures tire degradation, drivers' recent performance, overtaking, yellow flag events, and rivals' pit-stop decisions. We train agents with five Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms and compare them with a Quadratic Mixed-Integer Programming (QMIP) formulation that is optimal in deterministic single-driver settings. Without uncertainty or competition, all DRL methods except TRPO achieve near-optimal performance. With a full grid of competitors and stochastic race events, the ranking of DRL methods depends on the evaluation setting: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its recurrent variant are the only methods that improve on the QMIP both in fully simulated races and when the actual 2024 races are replayed. Averaged over eight circuits, PPO improves on the QMIP by 0.33 and 0.49 positions in the two settings and Recurrent PPO by less, and in the replay PPO finishes 0.66 positions ahead of the drivers' actual strategies simulated in the same races. The QMIP performs similarly to the other methods, even though it cannot anticipate yellow flag events. Finally, we use the trained PPO policy as a look-ahead decision-support tool that shows the strategist the distribution of race outcomes under each candidate pit-stop action. Applied retrospectively to eight 2024 races, the look-ahead identifies the laps where the actual decision, the recommendation, or a third action was preferable.
comment: 54 pages (main text and appendices). Code, data and trained models: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24361704

title: Surface Cues Over Structure: Probing LLM Behavior on Brain Connectivity Graphs
summary: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) provides a noninvasive view of functional interactions across the brain, which can be represented as connectivity graphs for neurological disease analysis. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being paired with such representations, yet it remains unclear whether they genuinely reason over the underlying connectivity or simply respond to surface-level cues that may trigger learned priors. We probe this question through a controlled study of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnosis from resting-state functional connectivity, isolating one factor at a time to determine what drives an LLM's predictions on brain connectivity graphs. Across six models, from small open-weight LLMs to a proprietary one, the same pattern holds: the results provide little evidence that predictions are consistently grounded in subject-specific connectivity. Brain region names, numeric formatting, and prompt framing shift what a model predicts without improving how well it separates ADHD subjects from Controls; perturbing the graph changes predictions no more for clinically meaningful regions than for random ones; and the models' own justifications contradict the values they cite, inconsistently interpreting the connectivity evidence provided to them. Across every probe, predictions follow the model's built-in class bias and the surface form of the prompt rather than the subject's connectivity, calling into question a premise underlying current LLM brain integration work. Our code is available at https://github.com/Roy025/ADHD-code.

title: Semigroup Hessian Estimates for Underdamped Langevin Dynamics
summary:
For the semigroup $e^{t\mathcal L}$ of the underdamped Langevin dynamics, we bound the Hessian $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ when $
abla f$ is uniformly bounded. When the potential is strongly convex outside a ball and has bounded second and third derivatives, and the damping rate is above an explicit threshold, the bounds on $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ decay exponentially in time with constants free of the dimension. The proof combines the Wasserstein contraction of the dynamics with a Bismut--Elworthy--Li formula for the degenerate noise. As an application, we prove the uniform-in-time error of the stochastic gradient UBU integrator, with an explicit coefficient of the numerical bias in the step size, proportional to the covariance of the stochastic gradient noise.

title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
comments: 20 pages (13 pages main text and a 7-page supplement), 8 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation
summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.
comment: 20 pages (13 pages main text and a 7-page supplement), 8 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation

title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
summary: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.

title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
comments: 20 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Code and data: https://github.com/labbip/noise_sd
summary: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Code and data: https://github.com/labbip/noise_sd

title: Semi-regular admixed arrays: asymptotic enumeration and when information is additive
summary: In genomic data analysis, admixed arrays are pairs of matrices recording the local ancestry and the allele at each position of the haplotypes of admixed individuals. We study two-way diploid admixed arrays with $N$ individuals and $P$ loci under two families of constraints: local ancestry tallies, which fix the number of ancestry assignments per individual, and ancestry-specific sums, which fix the allele count per locus and ancestry. These two constraint families correspond to summaries of admixed genetic data investigated in biomedical and genomic applications. In the semi-regular regime, where all tallies and sums are uniform, we use complex martingale techniques to derive asymptotic formulas for the number of doubly constrained arrays as $N$ and $P$ grow with bounded ratio, over the whole feasible region. The leading term is governed by the Shannon entropy of the frequencies of the four possible pairs of entries at a position of the two matrices; on the boundary one or two of them vanish, changing the Gaussian correction. We then ask whether the two families carry information additively, that is, whether an independence heuristic predicts the doubly constrained count up to a bounded factor. Measured against the smallest set of arrays defined by a constraint that each family implies on its own, additivity holds only on a set of measure zero. It includes an edge of the feasible region with correction factor $e^{-1/4}$, extending our earlier result at the symmetric point. Thus, how far the two summaries jointly narrow down individual-level ancestry and genotype configurations cannot generally be predicted from how far each does on its own.

title: Moonshine Conjecture Formalized
comments: 7 pages, 0 figures. A case study in Lean formalization, semantic trust, and repository versioning
summary:
The celebrated and intimidating Moonshine Conjecture has now been formalized in Lean. This achievement might suggest that, once a sufficiently large library compiles, the principal mathematical work is complete. This paper tells a less optimistic story.
  During our formalization project, we repeatedly encountered two problems that a formally checked proof alone does not settle: (1) whether the formal statements actually express the mathematics we humans expect, and (2) how that meaning survives as the repositories and their dependencies evolve.
  We argue that there is no magic pill that turns a large agent-produced library into mathematics a community can trust. Even after the proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, someone must judge whether the definitions and statements express the intended mathematics and whether future updates preserve that meaning. This work, even when done, can only be trusted. We must therefore return to the usual trust model: relying on the mathematical judgment of maintainers and expert communities.
  But semantic review is expensive, making it tempting to keep producing code and take successful kernel checks as sufficient grounds for trust. This shortcut accumulates semantic debt: definitions and results with unchecked mathematical interpretations are reused as foundations for further work. A library may keep compiling and produce the desired formal theorem while users lose track of which mathematical claims they can responsibly rely on.
  Reliable reuse is also a prerequisite for Terence Tao's vision of formal mathematics as something people can navigate, explain, learn from, and build with. This paper takes our work connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories for the Moonshine Conjecture as a case study of the challenges of reliable reuse as formal developments scale.
