title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
summary: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

title: On the convergence of greedy algorithms in one-dimensional Wasserstein space
summary: We study the convergence of the greedy algorithm for approximating a compact set by barycenters in metric spaces, in particular in the space of one-dimensional measures endowed with the 2-Wasserstein distance. To this end, we compare several metric $N$-widths, which measure the best error achievable with $N$-point barycenters, using either classical barycenters having nonnegative weights or signed barycenters, with weights of arbitrary sign summing to one. For the analysis we exploit that quantile functions embed the one-dimensional 2-Wasserstein space isometrically into a convex cone of $L^2(0,1)$, and barycenter sets correspond to nonlinear projections of convex or affine hulls. We prove, both in the algebraic and exponential case, that the convergence rate of the greedy algorithm using signed barycenters matches the one of the metric $N$-width defined with classical barycenters. We provide counterexamples showing that this fails for the other combinations.

title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making in Signed Networks
summary: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.

title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
summary: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework for SAR-related foundation models: five rating levels, six dimensions, and fine-grained criteria, with separate protocols for VFMs and VLMs. Beyond overall ratings, it yields interpretable multidimensional capability profiles and supports user-defined weighting, so rankings follow user priorities. Utilizing a fixed auxiliary multimodal large language model in combination with human review, we conduct a systematic meta-analysis and multidimensional assessment of 76 VFMs and 40 VLMs. In terms of SAR benchmark task performance under our framework, SAR-native VLMs do not significantly outperform remote sensing VLMs pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora in which SAR is one of several modalities. This lack of clear advantage is largely due to data availability: large-scale, high-quality, public annotated SAR data remain scarce, restricting both model and training-data scale for SAR-native models. The framework provides a structured basis for requirement-aware model selection and remains extensible as new models emerge.

title: Radio antipodal number for the Cartesian product of a complete graph and a path
comments: 16 pages, 1 figure. (This is the final version published in Congressus Numerantium)
summary: A radio antipodal labeling of a graph $G$ is a function $f$ that assigns a non negative integer to each vertex in such a way that for any pair of distinct vertices $x$ and $y$, the condition $|f(x)-f(y)| \geq d-d(x,y)$ is satisfied, where $d$ and $d(x,y)$ represent the diameter of graph $G$, and distance between $x$ and $y$ in graph $G$, respectively. The span of radio antipodal labeling $f$ is defined as $span(f) = \max\{|f(x)-f(y)| : x,y \in V(G)\}$. The radio antipodal number of graph $G$, denoted by $an(G)$, is defined as $an(G) := \min_{f}\{span(f)\}$ with minimum taken over all radio antipodal labelings $f$ of $G$. A radio antipodal labeling $f$ of $G$ is optimal if $span(f) = an(G)$. In this paper, we give the exact radio antipodal number of the Cartesian product of a complete graph and a path.
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure. (This is the final version published in Congressus Numerantium)

title: Dem2TA: Beyond Pixels, Towards Perception
summary: Task-oriented image signal processors (ISPs) adapt RAW-to-RGB processing for downstream perception. However, explicit demosaicing is often simplified, kept fixed, or optimized primarily for reconstruction quality, leaving this stage insufficiently integrated into task adaptation. We propose \textbf{Dem2TA}, a framework that incorporates fidelity-supervised demosaicing into the adaptation of the perception pipeline. Starting from a pretrained demosaicing model, we jointly adapt the reconstruction frontend and downstream network using reconstruction and task supervision, together with complementary semantic and task representation alignment. We then freeze the adapted frontend and jointly optimize a lightweight local ISP with the downstream model to refine task-specific rendering without changing the reconstructed linear RGB. Experiments on synthetic RAW detection and box-prompted segmentation demonstrate the effectiveness of representation-guided joint adaptation and subsequent local rendering. Evaluation on a manually verified real-capture dataset further supports transfer beyond synthetic inputs. Compared with TA-ISP on the same adapted foundation, Dem2TA improves detection AP by 0.46 points and segmentation IoU by 1.06 points on synthetic COCO RAW, and segmentation IoU by 0.63 points on real captures.

title: Parameterized Subset Sum for Integers and Solvable Permutation Groups
summary: We show that parameterized subset sum for binary-encoded integers belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2]$, where the parameter is the number of selected integers. This improves a result of Buss and Islam, who proved membership in $\mathsf{W}[3]$. The proof uses an fpt-reduction to weighted CNF satisfiability without changing the parameter. For every fixed integer $d\geq1$, we also show that parameterized subset sum for permutation groups of derived length $d$ belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2d]$. The proof combines positive CNFs for addition in small abelian groups with an affine decomposition of a solvable permutation action. This gives circuits of weft at most $2d$ and depth depending only on $d$ for product evaluation. For every fixed nilpotency class, we obtain the stronger bound $\mathsf{W}[2]$ by an fpt-reduction to subset sum in abelian permutation groups. The reduction uses Hall's polynomial coordinates in a free nilpotent group and the Magnus embedding. For nilpotent permutation groups without a fixed class bound, we prove $\mathsf{W}[2]$-hardness, already for permutation $2$-groups.

title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
summary: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bužek, Hillery, and Werner.

title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
summary: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.

title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
summary: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
summary: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.

title: Linear Convergence of Adaptive Accelerated Gradient Methods: A Unified Framework
summary: We establish a unified Lyapunov framework for adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives. Conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation ensure eventual linear convergence without assuming stepsize convergence. We verify these conditions for specified AdaNAG-G, smooth unconstrained AC-FGM, and AdaAGM policies and use them to design VC-FG and CC-FG. The verified adaptive main iterations require neither global smoothness nor strong-convexity parameters and avoid restart and backtracking. The framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound. Experiments on four smooth, strongly convex problem families illustrate complementary performance of the new methods.

title: Structure-preserving compression of Matrix Product States
summary: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control the growth of bond dimensions, but compression can break the conservation laws of the equation being solved. A truncation is not the flow of a Hermitian generator, so even a small truncation error can violate exact algebraic identities of the Schrödinger equation. For any matrix product state integrator that leaves the state in canonical form with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant after compression whenever the resulting scalar quadratic constraint equation admits a real root, without enlarging any bond dimension. Rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers when that correction fails. The geometry of the low-rank manifold provides sufficient conditions for conservation by the fixed-rank projected flow and bounds what corrections within a frozen center frame can achieve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories.

title: Neural variational Skyrmions as a topological benchmark: emergent symmetry, precision energies and KAN--MLP comparison
comments: 32 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24390286
summary: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time. We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.

title: Consensus of Consensus: Decentralized Consensus-Based Optimization
summary: We propose and analyze a decentralized variant of Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO) for the global minimization of continuous, possibly non-convex functions accessible only through a stochastic, possibly biased, zeroth-order oracle with bounded mean-squared error. The agents are split among $N$ units of an undirected communication network. Each unit evolves its swarm of $M$ agents towards a local tracking variable, which follows the network average of the local consensus points through one round of neighbour-to-neighbour communication via a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, without any central coordinator. We show that, under an explicit condition linking the drift and diffusion parameters to $M$, all agents reach consensus almost surely, at an exponential mean-square rate governed by the spectrum of the mixing matrix. Using a finite-agent quantitative Laplace principle, we prove that, for large $α$ and provided some agent visits a neighbourhood of the global minimizer with sufficient probability, the expected mean-squared distance of the swarm from the minimizer falls below any tolerance within an explicit number of iterations, at a rate that deteriorates for poorly connected networks. We verify this hitting assumption for a simplified dynamics. Experiments on benchmarks up to dimension $d=1000$, with stochastic objectives, and on a federated learning task demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

title: Scattering by two parallel semi--infinite arrays of sound--soft scatterers
summary: This article considers the scattering of an acoustic wave by two identical semi--infinite arrays of point scatterers which are positioned parallel to one another. The resulting system of scattering coefficients is formulated as a pair of coupled discrete Wiener--Hopf equations with a full $2\times2$ matrix kernel composed of two scalar kernel functions that represent interaction within the selected array and between the two arrays. Exploiting the symmetry of the two arrays, we introduce symmetric and antisymmetric components of the scattering coefficients, which decouple the matrix Wiener--Hopf system into two independent scalar problems with kernels given by the sum and difference of the two original kernel functions. The scalar Wiener--Hopf equations are then solved using the Wiener--Hopf technique in a very similar way to what has previously been used to solve the semi--infinite array problem. The original definitions of the two scalar kernels are represented by a lattice sum and practical evaluation techniques are discussed. Comparisons with previous work are also critically discussed. The resulting formulation provides an exact analytical solution to a coupled semi--infinite array problem and illustrates how symmetry can reduce a discrete matrix Wiener--Hopf problem to two scalar problems.

title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
summary: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

title: Additive cubes are avoidable by a non-uniform morphism of length $6$ over $\{0,a,b\}$ (with $b \ge 4$ and $\gcd(a,b) = 1$)
summary: We prove that additive cubes are avoidable over every ternary alphabet $\{0, a, b\}$ with $1 \le a < b$, $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, and $b \ge 4$, thereby solving and extending Rao's~(2015) conjecture from $b \ge 6$ down to $b \ge 4$. Our construction applies a single dual pair of parameterized non-uniform morphisms of image length at most~$6$ to the additive-cube-free word $\mathbf{w}$ of Cassaigne et al.~(2014). For $b \ge 10$, we prove that every additive square in the image is an abelian square, reducing additive cubes to abelian cubes; the absence of abelian cubes and the $24$ finite cases with $4 \le b \le 9$ are then certified via the finite-graph method of Jamet and Rosenfeld~(2026).

title: From Tokens to Pixels: Training-Free Guided Upsampling of Frozen CARL Features for Hyperspectral Imaging
comments: 17 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Code and result tables: https://gitlab.fb10.fh-dortmund.de/fb10-opensource/CARL-tokens-to-pixels
summary: Camera-agnostic foundation models such as CARL map spectral images from arbitrary sensors into a shared feature space, but deliver their features only on a token grid at one eighth of the input resolution. The usual bilinear interpolation blurs material boundaries over about one token and rounds off corners. We investigate how much spatial accuracy image-guided upsampling recovers for frozen CARL features without training the encoder or the upsampler. We compare joint bilateral upsampling (JBU), a guided filter and the pretrained AnyUp, each with the hyperspectral image or an RGB rendering as the guide. A hyperspectral ColorChecker dataset acquired specifically for this study, with model-independent reference geometry measured to sub-pixel precision, serves as the evaluation benchmark. JBU with the hyperspectral guide raises the Boundary IoU from 13 to 67 % and reduces the effective edge width of the features from 38 to 4 px, close to the resolution of the raw spectra. The effect occurs in all 24 patches of the ColorChecker and replicates on an additional recording. On placenta and oral cavity images, the feature edges also become markedly qualitatively sharper. For sharp, high-contrast boundaries, JBU is the most accurate and most economical method. On tissue with softer transitions, the pretrained AnyUp yields qualitatively sharper contours. An analysis of 78 simulated band configurations shows that the gain persists in every configuration as long as the head matches the configuration. Image-guided upsampling is thus a simple, training-free step for applications that use CARL frozen with linear heads.

title: How coalition size shapes bill cosponsorship in the U.S. Congress
summary: Legislation is built by coalitions, yet studied through pairwise ties. Using five decades of U.S. House and Senate cosponsorship (1973-2025), we represent each bill as a group. Prior ties to current members predict who joins better than ties to the sponsor, and group history (earlier co-appearance with pairs of those members) produces a larger likelihood gain than sponsor ties alone. Coalition formation therefore retains a social memory of earlier groups: cooperation is organized around relational histories embedded in the coalition already assembled, which sponsor-cosponsor ties alone cannot recover. Completed coalitions also recur and share subgroups more often than degree- and size-preserving nulls predict. Party sorting peaks in coalitions of a few dozen members; as Congress polarized, small coalitions retained their cross-party share while mid-size coalitions became more partisan. Women are over-represented chiefly in coalitions led by Democratic women, although same-gender sponsor matching is close to zero after adjustment.

title: Incentive-Based Regulatory Mechanism for Tariff Design in District Heating and Cooling Networks
summary: Low-temperature district heating and cooling networks exchange heat bidirectionally at near-ambient temperatures. When one supplier owns the shared loop, it controls both the tariff and the network temperature that sets every user's conversion efficiency. Existing price-cap and cost-based rules leave this non-price instrument unregulated and reach neither the first-best dispatch nor an explicit division of gains. This paper proposes a two-part, incentive-based tariff that anchors the supplier's lump-sum fee, per building and hour, to an audited outside alternative and divides the participation gains through one regulated share. We model a mixed-integer bilevel Stackelberg game in which the supplier sets hourly tariffs and the temperature regime, anticipating the buildings' co-optimization of electricity and thermal exchange. We prove that the mechanism attains the first-best welfare, posts the shadow price of the efficient dispatch as its tariff, keeps every building at or above its outside option every hour, and keeps the supplier solvent whenever operation adds surplus. A Belgian case study confirms these properties. The mechanism reproduces the centralized welfare whenever operation is worthwhile, declines to operate otherwise, holds the loop at its first-best temperature, and outperforms cap-based regulation and Ramsey pricing in welfare, user protection, and cost recovery.

title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
comments: 6 pages, 1 figure. Prepared for ESANN 2027. Code and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/CeciliaBotelho/ESANN-2026
summary: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Prepared for ESANN 2027. Code and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/CeciliaBotelho/ESANN-2026

title: Generalized Markov numbers and plane lattices
summary: We give new explicit constructions of lattice rules in the two-dimensional square and torus. It is well-known that uniformly distributed lattices (in the sense of low-discrepancy) arise from continued fractions with bounded partial denominators. We demonstrate how integers solutions of the generalized Markov equation $x^2+y^2+z^2 = kxyz-k+3$ give rise to such lattices.

title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
summary: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
summary: Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
summary: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
summary: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.

title: Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse
summary: Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.

title: Feasibility of Multifrequency Neural Network-Based Wave Inversion in Ultrasound Time-Harmonic Elastography
summary:
Ultrasound time-harmonic elastography (THE) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft-tissue stiffness. Relying on the same principle of time-harmonic shear wave excitation as established magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), THE offers full field-of-view stiffness mapping at short acquisition times and sub-second temporal resolution across organs. However, reconstruction of shear wave speed maps from acquired tissue wavefields remains challenging due to speckle noise and sparse spatial coverage of the lateral component.
  Deep learning methods have shown promising results for image reconstruction in transient-based ultrasound elastography modalities but remain unexplored in THE. In MRE, MF-ElastoNet, a 2D multifrequency neural network-based wave reconstruction method trained on synthetic physics-based wave data, has shown high generalizability across dynamic ranges and resolutions.
  We investigated the potential of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion for THE, by performing a first feasibility analysis. To this end, we adapted the processing pipeline of MF-ElastoNet from MRE to THE. We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
summary:
Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced.
  On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
summary: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
comments: 7 pages, 4 figures, contribution to the Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on QCD in Extreme Conditions (xQCD 2026), 14-17 July 2026, Busan, Korea
summary: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. We confirm this by comparing observables to analytically known values and to hybrid Monte Carlo results.
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, contribution to the Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on QCD in Extreme Conditions (xQCD 2026), 14-17 July 2026, Busan, Korea

title: Underwater Spectral Recovery via Multi-View Hyperspectral Imaging
comments: Preprint. Code and data can be shared upon publication. 27 pages (15 main, 12 appendix), 12 figures
summary: Underwater imaging suffers from wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering that distort scenes and obscure spectral signatures. While RGB restoration improves visual clarity, the outputs remain broadband and tied to the sensor's color space. We introduce a physically grounded framework that lifts underwater restoration to continuous spectral radiance using multi-view hyperspectral imaging. By representing continuous spectra via low-rank basis functions and leveraging multi-distance observations, our framework jointly constrains scene radiance and water parameters. We employ a robust sparse-to-dense pipeline: water parameters are estimated from consistent multi-view matches and then applied globally to invert the light transport model across the full images. Validated on physics-based synthetic data rendered via the Mitsuba 3 spectral path tracer, our method recovers physically meaningful radiance spectra and, as a downstream application, outperforms standard image restoration baselines.
comment: Preprint. Code and data can be shared upon publication. 27 pages (15 main, 12 appendix), 12 figures

title: Tackling Many-Body Coulomb Singularity by Randomization
summary: Many-body Coulomb dynamics is central to quantum chemistry and molecular simulation, yet the Coulomb singularity undermines both the standard error analysis and performance of product formulas. Even for the simple hydrogen ground state, the celebrated Trotter formulas converge more slowly than their nominal order, and going to higher order does not help. Randomization by itself does not resolve this. We show that conventional qDRIFT suffers the same loss of accuracy, and that for general initial states, the errors of both Trotter formulas and qDRIFT can decrease more slowly than any power of the number of time steps (logarithmically). To overcome these limitations, we introduce supersmoothing qDRIFT, a randomized product formula that turns a physical property of free particle propagation into an algorithmic resource. Our algorithm achieves an error bound that decreases linearly with the time step, uniformly over \textit{all} initial states and without any smoothness or energy assumptions. Combined with spatial discretization analysis, the resulting end-to-end gate count improves on those of qubitization and high-order Trotter formulas applied directly to the discretized Hamiltonian, despite first-order convergence in time. This work demonstrates new ways of utilizing continuum dynamics to achieve algorithmic advantage.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
comments: 10 pages of main text (76 pages including references and appendices). Accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.
comment: 10 pages of main text (76 pages including references and appendices). Accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026

title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
summary: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
summary:
We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ
  \lesssim_α
  ν^{1/α}
  \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $α$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $α$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

title: Hypercube LSH for approximate near neighbors
comments: v2 (Nov 2026) fixes an error in one of the branches of the main result
summary:
A celebrated technique for finding near neighbors for the angular distance involves using a set of random hyperplanes to partition the space into hash regions [Charikar, STOC 2002]. Experiments later showed that using a set of orthogonal hyperplanes, thereby partitioning the space into the Voronoi regions induced by a hypercube, leads to even better results [Terasawa and Tanaka, WADS 2007]. However, no theoretical explanation for this improvement was ever given, and it remained unclear how the resulting hypercube hash method scales in high dimensions.
  In this work, we provide explicit asymptotics for the collision probabilities when using hypercubes to partition the space. Vectors at angle $π/3$ collide with probability $(\sqrt{3}/π)^{d + o(d)}$ in dimension $d$, compared to $(2/3)^d$ for random hyperplanes, and near-parallel vectors collide with similar asymptotic probabilities in both cases. The limiting exponential base tends continuously to zero as the angle approaches $\fracπ{2}$ from below.
  For fixed near and far angular thresholds below $π/2$, these asymptotics determine the limiting LSH collision-probability ratio $ρ$. We further describe how to use hypercube LSH in practice. A direct partial-hypercube analysis gives a heuristic lattice-sieving time bound $2^{0.3347d+o(d)}$.
comment: v2 (Nov 2026) fixes an error in one of the branches of the main result

title: On the interplay between noise and curvature and its effect on optimization and generalization
summary: The speed at which one can minimize an expected loss using stochastic methods depends on two properties: the curvature of the loss and the variance of the gradients. While most previous works focus on one or the other of these properties, we explore how their interaction affects optimization speed. Further, as the ultimate goal is good generalization performance, we clarify how both curvature and noise are relevant to properly estimate the generalization gap. Realizing that the limitations of some existing works stems from a confusion between these matrices, we also clarify the distinction between the Fisher matrix, the Hessian, and the covariance matrix of the gradients.

title: Revisiting the Graph Isomorphism Problem with Semidefinite Programming
summary: It is well-known that two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $n$ vertices are isomorphic if and only if their compatibility graph, an auxiliary graph on $n^2$ vertices, contains a clique of order $n$. In this paper, we give an exact conic formulation of this clique problem. We show that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic if and only if a system of linear constraints over the cone of completely positive matrices is feasible. Since deciding membership in the completely positive cone is NP-hard, this formulation does not by itself yield an efficient algorithm. Relaxing complete positivity to positive semidefiniteness yields a semidefinite program whose infeasibility certifies that the two graphs are not isomorphic. We establish basic properties of this relaxation. Specifically, it is at least as strong as the necessary condition given by the Lovász $\vartheta$ number of the complement of the compatibility graph, it never admits a strictly feasible solution, and it is implied by the degree-two level of the Lasserre hierarchy applied to a natural integer formulation of graph isomorphism. In light of known lower bounds for the Lasserre hierarchy, the latter indicates that the relaxation cannot decide isomorphism for all pairs of graphs. We leave open the question of characterizing the pairs of graphs for which the relaxation is tight.

title: Space-Efficient Interior Point Method, with applications to Linear Programming and Maximum Weight Bipartite Matching
comments: ICALP 2023. This version corrects the pass bound for linear programs of treewidth $τ$ (the previous bound holds only when $m = O(n τ)$) and fixes several algorithms and proofs: the small-space Lewis weight computation, the structure of optimal solutions used for vertex cover, and the final matching step
summary:
We study the problem of solving linear programs in the streaming model. Given a constraint matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and vectors $b\in\mathbb{R}^m, c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we develop a space-efficient interior point method that optimizes solely on the dual program. To this end, we obtain efficient algorithms for various different problems. For general linear programs whose feasible region lies in a ball of radius $R$ and contains a ball of radius $r$ with known center, we can solve them in $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\log(mR^2\|c\|_2/(rε)))$ passes and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ space for an $ε$-approximate solution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most efficient LP solver in streaming with no polynomial dependence on $m$ for both space and passes. For bipartite graphs, we can solve the minimum vertex cover and maximum weight matching problems (with polynomially bounded integer weights) in $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m})$ passes and $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space.
  In addition to our space-efficient IPM, we also give algorithms for solving SDD systems and the isolation lemma in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space, which are the cornerstones for our graph results.

title: A Certified Reduced Basis Method for Linear Parametrized Parabolic Optimal Control Problems in Space-Time Formulation
summary: In this work, we propose to efficiently solve time dependent parametrized optimal control problems governed by parabolic partial differential equations through the certified reduced basis method. In particular, we will exploit an error estimator procedure, based on easy-to-compute quantities which guarantees a rigorous and efficient bound for the error of the involved variables. First, we propose analyzing the problem at hand, proving its well-posedness thanks to Ne\v cas - Babu\v ska theory in a space-time formulation. Then, we derive error estimators to apply a Greedy method during the offline stage, to perform, during the online stage, a Galerkin projection onto a low-dimensional space spanned by properly chosen high-fidelity solutions. We tested the error estimators on two model problems governed by a Graetz flow with physical and geometrical parametrization. The results have been compared to a previously proposed bound, based on the exact computation of the Babu\v ska inf-sup constant, in terms of reliability and computational costs. We remark that our findings still hold in the steady setting, and we also propose a brief insight for this simpler formulation.

title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for multi-layer ResNets in the mean-field regime
summary: Finding the optimal configuration of parameters in ResNet is a nonconvex minimization problem, but first-order methods often find the global optimum when the network is overparameterized and the training algorithm is run for sufficiently many iterations. We study this phenomenon in the mean-field regime, where the network can be described approximately by an ordinary integral equation (OIE) and the training process of ResNet becomes a gradient-flow partial differential equation (PDE). Under the condition that the activation function is $2$-homogeneous or partially $1$-homogeneous, we show that this gradient-flow PDE converges to the global minimum. This result suggests that if the ResNet is sufficiently large, first-order optimization methods can find global minimizers that fit the training data as well. Further, by controlling the generalization error, we prove that the gradient-flow PDE is stable with respect to its cost function, implying that a finite-sized but sufficiently large dataset drawn from the underlying data distribution can exhibit the properties of the continuous limit. We give lower bounds on the depth and width of the network for the gradient-flow approximation to hold. We also lower-bound the size of the training data set needed to attain accurate approximation.

title: The Stochastic Arrival Problem
summary: We study a new modification of the Arrival problem, which allows for nodes that exhibit random as well as controlled behaviour, in addition to switching nodes. We study the computational complexity of these extensions, building on existing work on Reachability Switching Games. In particular, we show for versions of the arrival problem involving just switching and random nodes it is \PP{}-hard to decide if their value is greater than a half and we give a PSPACE decision algorithm.

title: OpinionGPT: Modelling Explicit Biases in Instruction-Tuned LLMs
comments: 6 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, matching NAACL 24 proceedings version
summary: Instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently showcased remarkable ability to generate fitting responses to natural language instructions. However, an open research question concerns the inherent biases of trained models and their responses. For instance, if the data used to tune an LLM is dominantly written by persons with a specific political bias, we might expect generated answers to share this bias. Current research work seeks to de-bias such models, or suppress potentially biased answers. With this demonstration, we take a different view on biases in instruction-tuning: Rather than aiming to suppress them, we aim to make them explicit and transparent. To this end, we present OpinionGPT, a web demo in which users can ask questions and select all biases they wish to investigate. The demo will answer this question using a model fine-tuned on text representing each of the selected biases, allowing side-by-side comparison. To train the underlying model, we identified 11 different biases (political, geographic, gender, age) and derived an instruction-tuning corpus in which each answer was written by members of one of these demographics. This paper presents OpinionGPT, illustrates how we trained the bias-aware model and showcases the web application (available at https://opiniongpt.informatik.hu-berlin.de).
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, matching NAACL 24 proceedings version

title: QANAD: A Model-Driven Framework for Quantitative Analysis and Synthesis of Activity Diagrams via Probabilistic Model Checking
comments: Accepted version by the journal of Software and Systems Modeling (SoSyM)
summary: Probabilistic model checking is a widely used formal verification technique to automatically verify qualitative and quantitative QoS properties for probabilistic models, such as reliability, performance, and cost. However, devising suitable and representative models for systems of interest in model checkers, writing corresponding properties, and verifying them requires domain knowledge in probabilistic models, formal verification, and the target model checkers. This unavoidably makes model checking not easily accessible for researchers and engineers who may lack the required knowledge. Previous work has extended UML activity diagrams with probability and time, along with quality annotations, developed transformations from activity diagrams to probabilistic models which model checkers support, and implemented accompanying tools for automation. The research, however, is fragmented, informal, or not fully open, making its use, extension, and adaptation non-trivial. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce QANAD, a comprehensive verification framework for activity diagrams, that includes a new profile for probability, time, parameters, and quality annotations, a semantics interpretation of activity diagrams in Markov models variants (DTMCs, MDPs, and CTMCs) and their parametric versions, and a set of formal transformation rules from activity diagrams to the PRISM modelling language, supported by the leading model checkers PRISM and Storm. The theory underpinning QANAD has been realised into transformation implementation using model-driven engineering, enabling fully automated model transformation with automated verification using (parametric) probabilistic model checking and semi-automated synthesis. We demonstrate QANAD on a case study where multiple robots are used for delivery in a hospital environment and evaluated six other examples from the literature.
comment: Accepted version by the journal of Software and Systems Modeling (SoSyM)

title: Super Guarding and Dark Rays in Art Galleries
comments: 24 pages, 16 figures, 10 references. v4: final journal version, Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science, vol. 28:3 #22 (2026)
summary: We explore an Art Gallery variant where each point of a polygon must be seen by k guards, and guards cannot see through other guards. Surprisingly, even covering convex polygons under this variant is not straightforward. For example, covering every point in a triangle k=4 times (a 4-cover) requires 5 guards, and achieving a 10-cover requires 12 guards. Our main result is tight bounds on k-covering a convex polygon of n vertices, for all k and n. The proofs of both upper and lower bounds are nontrivial. We also obtain bounds for simple polygons, leaving tight bounds an open problem.
comment: 24 pages, 16 figures, 10 references. v4: final journal version, Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science, vol. 28:3 #22 (2026)

title: Secure Distributed Matrix Multiplication with Precomputation
summary:
We consider secure distributed matrix multiplication, in which a user computes the product of two matrices with the help of honest-but-curious servers, any $T$ of which may collude. Using the outer-product partition, the matrices are split into $K$ and $L$ blocks and hidden by random masks. Assuming the user has precomputed the products of the random matrices, we develop methods that use this precomputation to reduce the number of servers required.
  Polynomial codes are designed through degree tables, whose distinct entries count the servers. We show that precomputation can reduce the minimum number of servers by designing degree tables specifically for this setting. For Gap Additive Secure Polynomial (GASPr) codes, we give a precise formula and show that it is monotone in the chain length $r$, so only the extremes GASP_small and GASP_big matter. We also prove lower bounds attained by GASP_small in several regimes. Consequently, any fraction of colluding servers below one can be tolerated, compared to the threshold of one half without precomputation, and the order of the total computational complexity decreases when the colluders are a fixed fraction of the servers. We show that no existing construction uses fewer servers than the better of GASP_small and GASP_big once the mask products are precomputed.
  We introduce Gap-Reduced Additive Secure Polynomial (GRASP) codes, which retain a single interval for the mask degrees while selecting the information degrees carefully. For $K = T = 4$ and every $L \geq 3$, we give an explicit GRASP code that uses one fewer server than every GASPr code and is within two servers of optimal. For large $T$, the configuration becomes an integer packing problem independent of $T$, and the number of servers saved by GRASP over GASPr grows quadratically in $K$ and $L$.

title: H(curl)-based approximation of the Stokes problem with slip boundary conditions
summary: Reformulating the incompressible Stokes equations with the velocity sought in H(curl) has recently emerged as a promising approach for the design of helicity-preserving schemes in magnetohydrodynamics and pressure-robust finite element methods on polygonal meshes. A key challenge in this setting, however, is the treatment of Navier slip boundary conditions. In this paper, we overcome this difficulty by recasting the slip condition as a Robin boundary condition and proving well-posedness (up to a finite-dimensional kernel) of the resulting continuous problem. We further identify the geometric and regularity assumptions on the domain and the exact solution under which the classical Stokes solution is recovered. Finally, we study a finite element Galerkin discretization, establishing stability and a priori error estimates. Numerical experiments validate the optimal convergence rates predicted by the theory.

title: A polytopal discontinuous Galerkin method for the pseudo-stress formulation of the unsteady Stokes problem
summary: This work aims to construct and analyze a discontinuous Galerkin method on polytopal grids (PolydG) to solve the pseudo-stress formulation of the unsteady Stokes problem. The pseudo-stress variable is introduced due to the growing interest in non-Newtonian flows and coupled interface problems, where stress assumes a fundamental role. The space-time discretization of the problem is achieved by combining the PolydG approach with the implicit theta-method time integration scheme. For both the semi- and fully-discrete problems we present a detailed stability analysis. Moreover, we derive convergence estimates for the fully discrete space-time discretization. A set of verification tests is presented to verify the theoretical estimates and the application of the method to cases of engineering interest.

title: Automatic Detection of LLM-Generated Code: A Comparative Case Study of Contemporary Models Across Function and Class Granularities
comments: Submitted to a journal for publication. This is the version after major revision round 2
summary:
The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation risks incorporating vulnerable code into software systems. Existing detectors face two critical limitations: a lack of systematic cross-model validation and opaque "black box" operation. We address this through a comparative study of code generated by four distinct LLMs: GPT-3.5, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-OSS.
  Analyzing 14,485 Python functions and 11,913 classes from the CodeSearchNet dataset, we generated corresponding code with all four LLMs. Using interpretable software metrics, we trained CatBoost classifiers for each configuration. Our analysis reveals that granularity effects dominate model differences by a factor of 8.6, with negligible feature overlap, indicating that function-level and class-level detection rely on fundamentally disjoint structural signatures.
  We discover critical granularity-dependent inversions: while modern models (Claude, GPT-OSS) are more detectable at the class level, GPT-3.5 is an anomaly that uniquely excels at the function level. SHAP analysis identifies the Comment-to-Code Ratio as the sole universal discriminator. However, its predictive magnitude varies drastically across models, explaining why detectors trained on specific LLMs fail to generalize.
  Our findings demonstrate that GPT-3.5's exceptional detectability (AUC-ROC 0.96) is unrepresentative of contemporary models (AUC-ROC approximately between 0.68 and 0.80). Robust detection requires moving beyond single-model studies to account for substantial diversity in structural fingerprints across architectures and granularities.
comment: Submitted to a journal for publication. This is the version after major revision round 2

title: A Chinese Continuous Sign Language Dataset Based on Complex Environments
summary: The current bottleneck in continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) research lies in the fact that most publicly available datasets are limited to laboratory environments or television program recordings, resulting in a single background environment with uniform lighting, which significantly deviates from the diversity and complexity found in real-life scenarios. To address this challenge, we have constructed a new, large-scale dataset for Chinese continuous sign language (CSL) based on complex environments, termed the complex environment - chinese sign language dataset (CE-CSL). This dataset encompasses 5,988 continuous CSL video clips collected from daily life scenes, featuring more than 70 different complex backgrounds to ensure representativeness and generalization capability. To tackle the impact of complex backgrounds on CSLR performance, we propose a time-frequency network (TFNet) model for continuous sign language recognition. This model extracts frame-level features and then utilizes both temporal and spectral information to separately derive sequence features before fusion, aiming to achieve efficient and accurate CSLR. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves significant performance improvements on the CE-CSL, validating its effectiveness under complex background conditions. Additionally, our proposed method has also yielded highly competitive results when applied to three publicly available CSL datasets.

title: Faster algorithms for packing forests in graphs and related problems
comments: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2409.14881
summary:
We consider several problems related to packing forests in graphs. The first one is to find $k$ edge-disjoint forests of maximum size in a directed graph $G$ such that the indegree of each vertex in these forests is at most $k$. We describe a min-max characterization for this problem and show that it can be solved in almost linear time for fixed $k$, extending the algorithm of [Gabow, 1995]. Specifically, the complexity is $O(k δm \log n)$, where $n, m$ are the numbers of vertices and edges in $G$, respectively, and $δ= \max\{1, k - k_G\}$, where $k_G$ is the edge connectivity of the graph. Using our solution to this problem, we obtain algorithms for two applications:
  (1) The $k$-forest problem: find $k$ forests in an undirected graph $G$ maximizing the number of edges in their union. We show how to solve this problem in $O(k^3 \min\{kn, m\} \log^2 n + k \cdot{\rm MAXFLOW}(m, m) \log n)$ time, breaking the $O_k(n^{3/2})$ complexity barrier of previously known approaches.
  (2) The Directed edge-connectivity augmentation problem: find a smallest set of directed edges whose addition to the given directed graph makes it strongly $k$-connected. We give a deterministic algorithm with complexity $O(k δm \log n)+T_{\rm split}$, where $T_{\rm split}$ is the time to split off one vertex in a graph with $O(m+δn)$ edges while preserving strong connectivity among the original vertices. For Eulerian directed graphs, the total complexity is $O(k δm \log n)$. A similar approach solves the undirected version of the problem in $O(k δm \log n)$ time.

title: Functional Flexibility in Generative AI Interfaces: Text Editing with LLMs through Conversations, Toolbars, and Prompts
comments: Just submitted. This is the author's version of the work
summary: Many recent user interfaces (UIs) promise great flexibility via access to Large Language Models (LLMs) through prompting. This shifts efforts in accessing functionality from developers to users. However, is a maximum of functional flexibility always beneficial? We find: no -- and develop Functional Flexibility as a concept by reflecting on our long-term exploration of integrating LLMs into a text editor: In a prompt-elicitation survey, people (N=121) envisioned elaborate prompts for delegating flexible tasks to AI. In contrast, when interacting with a prototype (N=10), users preferred short command-like prompts, as prompting repeated functionality is tedious. Another prototype offered such commands in a toolbar, in addition to flexible prompting, leading users (N=12) to dynamically work with both. We contribute Functional Flexibility as a theoretical construct with analytical, critical, and constructive value. Overall, we encourage designing UIs for generative AI that go beyond free text prompting by explicitly considering functional flexibility in design.
